entries.fe5a0a98f2d96a663483c9d537a57d2dc498cd47: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16973" type="x-p"/> Therefore snares - As thou hast dealt with others, so has God, in his retributive providence, dealt with thee. As thou hast spoiled, so art thou spoiled. Thou art taken in a net from which thou canst not escape. There is an allusion here to the hunting of the elephant: he is driven into an inclosure in the woods, passing from strait to strait, till brought into a narrow point, from which he cannot escape; and then his consternation is great, and his roaring terrible. God hath hunted thee down, as men hunt down those wild and dangerous beasts. See on <reference osisRef="Job.18.21">Job 18:21</reference> (note).
entries.95e99529c53489899959dd9f5defc5f80d7e5bea: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16974" type="x-p"/> Or darkness, that thou canst not see - The sense of this passage, in the connection that the particle or gives it with the preceding verse, is not easy to be ascertained. To me it seems very probable that a letter has been lost from the first word; and that או o which we translate Or, was originally אור or Light. The copy used by the Septuagint had certainly this reading; and therefore they translate the verse thus: Το φως σοι εις σκοτος απεβη; Thy Light is changed into darkness; that is, Thy prosperity is turned into adversity. <div eID="gen16974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16975" type="x-p"/> Houbigant corrects the text thus: instead of או חשך לא תראה o chosech lo tireh, or darkness thou canst not see, he reads חשך לא אור תראה chosech lo or tireh, darkness, not light, shalt thou behold; that is, Thou shalt dwell in thick darkness. Mr. Good translates: "Or darkness which thou canst not penetrate, and a flood of waters shall cover thee." Thou shalt either be enveloped in deep darkness, or overwhelmed with a flood. <div eID="gen16975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16976" type="x-p"/> The versions all translate differently; and neither they nor the MSS. give any light, except what is afforded by the Septuagint. Coverdale is singular: Shuldest thou then send darcknesse? Shulde not the water floude runne over the? Perhaps the meaning is: "Thou art so encompassed with darkness, that thou canst not see thy way; and therefore fallest into the snares and traps that are laid for thee."
entries.0e27f6254e9b4926b20c6c7369213842540dc2f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16977" type="x-p"/> Is not God in the height of heaven? - It appears, from this and the following verses, that Eliphaz was attributing infidel and blasphemous speeches or sentiments to Job. As if he had said: "Thou allowest that there is a God, but thou sayest that he is infinitely exalted above the heavens and the stars, and that there is so much dense ether and thick cloud between his throne and the earth, that he can neither see it nor its inhabitants." These were sentiments which Job never held, and never uttered; but if a man be dressed in a bear's skin, he may be hunted and worried by his own dogs. Job's friends attribute falsities to him, and then dilate upon them, and draw inferences from them injurious to his character. Polemic writers, both in theology and politics, often act in this way.
entries.6147b9acebefc95a6043579d0cd5afd71138e37f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16978" type="x-p"/> He walketh in the circuit of heaven - He confines himself to those infinitely exalted regions and cares nothing for the inhabitants of the earth.
entries.4b0cc8d7765310ffb2980966c1b2bb01d4c5a1d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16979" type="x-p"/> Hast thou marked the old way - This is supposed to be another accusation; as i! he had said, "Thou hollowest the same way that the wicked of old have walked in." Here is an evident allusion to the Flood, as is particularly noted in the next verse.
entries.769865aee9891fa65d15d4d861028cd10142006d: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16980" type="x-p"/> Whose foundation was overflown with a flood - The unrighteous in the days of Noah, who appear to have had an abundance of all temporal good, (<reference osisRef="Job.22.18">Job 22:18</reference>), and who surpassed the deeds of all the former wicked, said in effect to God, Depart from us. And when Noah preached unto them the terrors of the Lord, and the necessity of repentance, they rejected his preaching with, What can the Almighty do for us? Let him do his worst; we care not for him, <reference osisRef="Job.22.17">Job 22:17</reference>. For למו lamo, to Them, the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic have evidently read לנו lanu, to Us. This reading quotes their own saying; the former reading narrates it in the third person. The meaning, however, is the same.
entries.b564659990cd0fe5a9927a81dfc56f39ff7e2ec3: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16981" type="x-p"/> But the counsel of the wicked is far from me - Sarcastically quoting Job's words, <reference osisRef="Job.21.14">Job 21:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference>. Job, having in the preceding chapter described the wicked, who said unto the Almighty, "Depart from us," etc., adds, But the counsel of the wicked is far from me. Eliphaz here, having described the impious, among whom he evidently ranks Job, makes use of the same expression, as if he had said, "Thank God, I have no connection with you nor your companions, nor is my mind contaminated by your creed."
entries.b26f8a667a8d667524bf9b3ac79e9e1a6f6dc487: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16982" type="x-p"/> The righteous see it, and are glad - They see God's judgments on the incorrigibly wicked, and know that the Judge of all the earth does right; hence they rejoice in all the dispensations of his providence.
entries.bf6812715341629cec63b9f364f6ee927bcd2ecc: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16983" type="x-p"/> Whereas our substance is not cut down - We, who fear the Lord, still continue in health and peace; whereas they who have departed from him are destroyed even to their very remnant. Mr. Good thinks that קימנו kimanu, which we translate our substance, is the same as the Arabic (Arabic) our people or tribe; and hence he translates the clause thus: "For our tribe is not cut off; while even the remnant of these a conflagration consumed." The reference here is supposed to be to the destruction of the men of Sodom and Gomorrah. A judgment by a flood took off the world of the ungodly in the days of Noah. Their remnant, those who lived in the same ungodly way, were taken off by a judgment of fire, in the days of Lot. Eliphaz introduces these two examples in order to terrify Job into a compliance with the exhortation which immediately follows.
entries.8339923c40f1bdb98e1c854c4328e28bebe3e740: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16984" type="x-p"/> Acquaint now thyself with him - Perhaps the verb הסכן hasken should be translated here, treasure up, or lay up. Lay up or procure an interest now with him, and be at peace. Get the Divine favor, and then thou wilt be at peace with God, and have happiness in thy own soul. <div eID="gen16984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16985" type="x-p"/> Thereby good shalt come unto thee - בהם bahem, "in them," shall good come unto thee. That is, in getting an interest in the Divine favor, and in having thy soul brought into a state of peace with him; thereby, in them, that is, these two things, good will come unto thee. First, thou wilt have an interest in his favor, from which thou mayest expect all blessings; and, secondly, from his peace in thy conscience thou wilt feel unutterable happiness. Get these blessings now, for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth. Reader, hast thou these blessings?
entries.0666bbfed55102955629847757483dd041c4f79b: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen16985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16986" type="x-p"/> Receive, I pray thee, the law from his mouth - Some, who wish to place Job before the law given by Moses, say that this means the Noahic precepts; others, that the law of nature is intended! Stuff and vanity! The allusion is plainly to the law given by God to the children of Israel, called here by way of emphasis, תורה torah, the Law, which contained אמריו amaraiv, his Words, the words or sayings of God himself; consequently, it is not the Noahic precepts, nor the law of nature, neither of which were ever written or registered as the words of God's mouth.
entries.c2bb080f50b7f27bd0cb496f6ebaf66f8384eda2: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen16986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16987" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt be built up - God will restore thee to thy wonted state of prosperity; and thou shalt again have a household, not only of servants, but of children also. So much may be Implied in the words, Thou shalt be Built Up. See my sermon on <reference osisRef="Job.22.21-Job.22.23">Job 22:21-23</reference>.
entries.309c80fba6a8bff6d1e4adb06592d3999e9c4f95: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen16987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16988" type="x-p"/> Then shalt thou lay up gold as dust - The original is not fairly rendered in this translation, ושית על עפר בצר veshith al aphar batser, which Montanus renders: Et pone super pulverem munitionem, "And fix a tower upon the dust;" ובצור נחלים אופיר ubetsur nechalim Ophir, et in petra torrentes Ophir, "and in the rock, the torrents of Ophir." The Vulgate is widely different: Dabit pro terra silicem, et pro silice torrentes aureos, "He will give thee flint for earth: and torrents of gold for flint;" which Calmet thus paraphrases: "Instead of brick thou shalt build with solid stone; and for ornaments, instead of stone as formerly, thou shalt have massive gold!" All the versions are different. Mr. Good translates: "Then count thou treasure as dust: then shall he make fountains to gush forth amidst the rocks." <div eID="gen16988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16989" type="x-p"/> Coverdale is different from all: We shal give the an harvest which, in plenty and abundance, shal exceade the dust of the earthe, and the golde of Ophir like ryver stones.
entries.885ebd4e2430897fa35e800d6c541622c8ef1775: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen16989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16990" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt have plenty of silver - Here again the versions and critics vary. The critics may disagree; but the doctrine of Eliphaz is sufficiently plain: "To those whom God loves best he gives the most earthly good. The rich and the great are his high favorites: the poor and the distressed he holds for his enemies." In the above verses there seems to be a reference to the mode of obtaining the precious metals: <div eID="gen16990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16991" type="x-p"/> 1. Gold in dust; <div eID="gen16991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16992" type="x-p"/> 2. Gold in streams from the hills and mountains; <div eID="gen16992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16993" type="x-p"/> 3. Silver in mines; כסף תועפות keseph toaphoth, "silver of giddiness," of mines so deep as to make one giddy by looking into them. See Mr. Good.
entries.b5732c2ae0748e38f7f62b91007a52bf2d8d18fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen16993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16994" type="x-p"/> For then shalt thou have thy delight - Thou shalt know, from thy temporal prosperity, that God favors thee; and for his bounty thou shalt be grateful. How different is this doctrine from that of St. Paul and St. John! "Being justified by faith, we have peace with God, through our Lord Jesus." "Because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father!" "The Spirit himself beareth witness with our spirits that we are the children of God." "We glory in tribulation also, knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope maketh not ashamed, because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost, which is given unto us." "We love him because he first loved us." Tribulation itself was often a mark of God's favor.
entries.8e58ad758e816efa89d8a68d0b5363299af325d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen16994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16995" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt make thy prayer unto him - תעתיר tatir, thou shalt open or unbosom thyself. And when the heart prays, God hears; and the person, being blessed, vows fidelity, prays on, is supported, and enabled to pay his vows.
entries.2fad9cf05c561ce6ff77eb4ebae96ee52566412e: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen16995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16996" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt also decree a thing - Whatsoever thou purposest in his strength, thou shalt be enabled to accomplish.
entries.5e00763173713556b713a1eb426b76a9c4d647be: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen16996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16997" type="x-p"/> When men are cast down - There is a great difficulty in this verse; the sense, however, is tolerably evident, and the following is nearly a literal version: When they shall humble themselves, thou shalt say, Be exalted, or, there is exaltation: for the down-cast of eye he will save. The same sentiment as that of our Lord, "He that exalteth himself shall be abased; but he that humbleth himself shall be exalted."
entries.9249d451c7d8760da9d894399773e53fe8b00cdb: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen16997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16998" type="x-p"/> He shall deliver the island of the innocent - The word אי ai, which we translate island, is most probably the Arabic particle (Arabic) whosoever, whatsoever, any, whosoever he may be, as (Arabic) ai rajuli, whatsoever man he may be. And it is most probable that both words are Arabic, (Arabic) or (Arabic) any innocent, chaste, pure, or holy person; for the word has the same meaning both in Hebrew and Arabic. The text may therefore be translated, He shall deliver every innocent person: He, the innocent person, shall be delivered by the pureness of thy hands; i.e., as thou lovest justice, so thou wilt do justice. Instead of כפיך cappeyca, thy hands, the Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic have read כפיו cappaiv, his or their hands. Mr. Good thinks that אי ai signifies house, as (Arabic) and (Arabic) in Arabic signify to reside, to have a home, etc.; and therefore translates the passage thus: "The house of the innocent shall be delivered; and delivered by the pureness of thy hands." The reader may adopt which he pleases; but the word island must be given up, as it cannot make any consistent sense. <div eID="gen16998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16999" type="x-p"/> Thus ends Eliphaz the Temanite, who began with a tissue of the bitterest charges, continued with the most cruel insinuations, and ended with common-place exhortations to repentance, and promises of secular blessings in consequence: and from his whole speech scarcely can one new or important maxim be derived. Blessed be God for Moses and the prophets! for Jesus, the evangelists and the apostles! Their trumpet gives no uncertain sound: but by that of Job's friends who can prepare himself for the battle?  <chapter eID="Job.22"/> <div eID="gen16999" type="x-p"/>

entries.8c22c34bb0b544caa640272c2ba31a24133a8d7d: <reference osisRef="Job.22.1-Job.5.1">Job 22:1-5   1</reference>  Then began Eliphaz the Temanite, and said:   2  Is a man profitable unto God? <div eID="gen7825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7826" type="x-p"/> No, indeed! the intelligent man is profitable to himself.   3  Hath the Almighty any profit if thou art righteous, <div eID="gen7826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7827" type="x-p"/> Or gain if thou strivest to walk uprightly?   4  Will He reprove thee for thy fear of God, <div eID="gen7827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7828" type="x-p"/> Will He go with thee into judgment?   5  Is not thy wickedness great, <div eID="gen7828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7829" type="x-p"/> Thine iniquities infinite? <div eID="gen7829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7830" type="x-p"/> The verb סכן, in the signification to be profitable, is peculiar to the book of Job (although also סכן and סכנת elsewhere, according to its primary signification, does not differ from מועיל, מועילה, by which it is explained by Kimchi); the correct development of the notion of this verb is to be perceived from the <hi type="italic">Hiph.,</hi> which occurs in <reference osisRef="Job.21.21">Job 21:21</reference> in this speech of Eliphaz (vid., Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>.): it signifies originally, like שׁכן, Arab. <hi type="italic">skn</hi>, to rest, dwell, especially to dwell beside one another, then to become accustomed to one another (comp. שׁכן, a neighbour, and Arab. <hi type="italic">sakanun</hi>, a friend, confidant), and to assist one another, to be serviceable, to be profitable; we can say both סכנתּי, I have profit, <reference osisRef="Job.34.9">Job 34:9</reference>, and סכן, it is profitable, <reference osisRef="Job.15.3">Job 15:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.35.3">Job 35:3</reference>, here twice with a personal subj., and first followed by ל, then with the על usual also elsewhere in later prose (e.g., טוב על,   <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.2">1Ch 13:2</reference>, comp. <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.10.3">Job 10:3</reference>, to be pleasant) and poetry, which gladly adopts Aramaisms (as here and <reference osisRef="Ps.16.6">Psa 16:6</reference>, שׁפר על, well-pleased), instead of ל, whence here עלימו, as <reference osisRef="Job.20.23">Job 20:23</reference>, pathetic for עליו. The question, which is intended as a negative, is followed by the negative answer (which establishes its negative meaning) with כּי; משׂכּיל is, like <reference osisRef="Ps.14.2">Psa 14:2</reference>, the intelligent, who wills and does what is good, with an insight into the nature of the extremes in morality, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.1.3">Pro 1:3</reference> independent morality which rests not merely on blind custom is called מוסר השׂכל. היה חפץ ל, it is to the interest of any one (different from <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>, vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.21.21">Job 21:21</reference>), and היה בצע ל, it is to the gain of any one (prop. the act of cutting, cutting off, i.e., what one tears in pieces), follow as synonyms of סכן. On the Aramaizing doubling of the first radical in the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. תתּם (instead of תתם), vid., Ges. §67, rem. 8, comp. 3. It is translated <hi type="italic">an lucrum</hi> (<hi type="italic">ei</hi>) <hi type="italic">si integras facias vias tuas.</hi> The meaning of the whole strophe is mainly determined according to the rendering of המיּראתך (like המבינתך, <reference osisRef="Job.39.26">Job 39:26</reference>, with Dechî, and as an exception with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, not removed to the place of the <hi type="italic">Metheg;</hi> vid., <hi type="italic">Psalter,</hi> ii. 491, Anm. 1). If the suff. is taken objectively (from fear of thee), e.g., Hirz., we have the following line of thought: God is neither benefited by human virtue nor injured by human sin, so that when He corrects the sinner He is turning danger from himself; He neither rewards the godly because He is benefited by his piety, nor punishes the sinner because by his sinning he threatens Him with injury. Since, therefore, if God chastises a man, the reason of it is not to be found in any selfish purpose of God, it must be in the sin of the man, which is on its own account worthy of punishment. But the logical relation in which <reference osisRef="Job.22.5">Job 22:5</reference> stands to <reference osisRef="Job.22.4">Job 22:4</reference> does not suit this: perhaps from fear of thee ... ? no, rather because of thy many and great sins! Hahn is more just to this relation when he explains: “God has no personal profit to expect from man, so that, somewhat from fear, to prevent him from being injurious, He should have any occasion to torment him with sufferings unjustly.” But if the personal profit, which is denied, is one that grows out of the piety of the man, the personal harm, which is denied as one which God by punishment will keep far from Himself, is to be thought of as growing out of the sin of the man; and the logical relation of <reference osisRef="Job.22.5">Job 22:5</reference> to <reference osisRef="Job.22.4">Job 22:4</reference> is not suited to this, for. <reference osisRef="Job.22.5">Job 22:5</reference> assigns the reason of the chastisement to the sin, and denies, as it runs, not merely any motive whatever in connection with the sin, but that the reason can lie in the opposite of sin, as it appears according to Job’s assertion that, although guiltless, he is still suffering from the wrath of God. <div eID="gen7830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7831" type="x-p"/> Thus, then, the suff. of המיראתך is to be taken subjectively: on account of thy fear of God, as Eliphaz has used יראתך twice already, <reference osisRef="Job.4.6">Job 4:6</reference>; Job 15:4. By this subjective rendering <reference osisRef="Job.22.4">Job 22:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.22.5">Job 22:5</reference> form a true antithesis: Does God perhaps punish thee on account of thy fear of God? Does He go (on that account) with thee into judgment? No (it would be absurd to suppose that); therefore thy wickedness must be great (in proportion to the greatness of thy suffering), and thy misdeeds infinitely many. If we now look at what precedes, we shall have to put aside the thought drawn into <reference osisRef="Job.22.2">Job 22:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.22.3">Job 22:3</reference> by Ewald (and also by Hahn): whether God, perhaps with the purpose of gaining greater advantage from piety, seeks to raise it by unjustly decreed suffering; for this thought has nothing to indicate it, and is indeed certainly false, but on account of the force of truth which lies in it (there is a decreeing of suffering for the godly to raise their piety) is only perplexing. <div eID="gen7831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7832" type="x-p"/> First of all, we must inquire how it is that Eliphaz begins his speech thus. All the exhortations to penitence in which the three exhaust themselves, rebound from Job without affecting him. Even Eliphaz, the oldest among them, full of a lofty, almost prophetic consciousness, has with the utmost solicitude allured and terrified him, but in vain. And it is the cause of God which he brings against him, or rather his own well-being that he seeks, without making an impression upon him. Then he reminds him that God is in Himself the all-sufficient One; that no advantage accrues to Him from human uprightness, since His nature, existing before and transcending all created things, can suffer neither diminution nor increase from the creature; that Job therefore, since he remains inaccessible to that well-meant call to penitent humiliation, has refused not to benefit Him, but himself; or, what is the reverse side of this thought (which is not, however, expressed), that he does no injury to Him, only to himself. And yet in what except in Job’s sin should this decree of suffering have its ground? If it is a self-contradiction that God should chastise a man because he fears Him, there must be sin on the side of Job; and indeed, since the nature of the sin is to be measured according to the nature of the suffering, great and measureless sin. This logical necessity Eliphaz now regards as real, without further investigation, by opening out this bundle of sins in the next strophe, and reproaching Job directly with that which Zophar, <reference osisRef="Job.20.19-Job.20.21">Job 20:19-21</reference>, aiming at Job, has said of the רשׁע. In the next strophe he continues, with כי <hi type="italic">explic.:  </hi>
entries.f79026bbefb6a7a846e61876a29e8f49f0827080: <reference osisRef="Job.22.6-Job.9.6">Job 22:6-9   6</reference>  For thou distrainedst thy brother without cause, <div eID="gen7832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7833" type="x-p"/> And the clothes of the naked thou strippedst off.   7  Thou gavest no water to the languishing, <div eID="gen7833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7834" type="x-p"/> And thou refusedst bread to the hungry.   8  And the man of the arm-the land was his, <div eID="gen7834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7835" type="x-p"/> And the honourable man dwelt therein.   9  Thou sentest widows away empty, <div eID="gen7835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7836" type="x-p"/> And the arms of the orphan are broken. <div eID="gen7836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7837" type="x-p"/> The reason of exceeding great suffering most be exceeding great sins. Job must have committed such sins as are here cited; therefore Eliphaz directly attributes guilt to him, since he thinks thus to tear down the disguise of the hypocrite. The strophe contains no reference to the Mosaic law: the compassionate Mosaic laws respecting duties towards widows and orphans, and the poor who pledge their few and indispensable goods, may have passed before the poet’s mind; but it is not safe to infer it from the expression. As specific Mohammedan commandments among the wandering tribes even in the present day have no sound, so the poet dare not assume, in connection with the characters of his drama, any knowledge, of the Sinaitic law; and of this he remains conscious throughout: their standpoint is and remains that of the Abrahamic faith, the primary commands (later called the ten commands of piety, el-felâhh) of which were amply sufficient for stigmatizing that to which this strophe gives prominence as sin. It is only the force of the connection of the matter here which gives the <hi type="italic">futt.</hi> which follow כי a retrospective meaning. חבל is connected either with the accusative of the thing for which the pledge is taken, as in the law, which meets a response in the heart, Exo 22:25.; or with the accus. of the person who is seized, as here אחיך; or, if this is really (as Bär asserts) a mistake that has gained a footing, which has Codd. and old printed editions against it, rather אחיך. lxx, Targ., Syr., and Jer. read the word as plural. ערוּמים (from ערום), like γυμνοί, Jam 2:15, <hi type="italic">nudi</hi> (comp. Seneca, <hi type="italic">de beneficiis,</hi> v. 13: <hi type="italic">si quis male vestitum et pannosum videt, nudum se vidisse dicit</hi>), are, according to our mode of expression, the half-naked, only scantily (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.20.2">Isa 20:2</reference>) clothed.
entries.0da26af44f41b33ea8bec7fb7a6d85cbc3047b09: <reference osisRef="Job.22.10-Job.11.10">Job 22:10-11 10</reference>  Therefore snares are round about thee, <div eID="gen7838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7839" type="x-p"/> And fear terrifieth thee suddenly; 11  Or percievest thou not the darkness, <div eID="gen7839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7840" type="x-p"/> And the overflow of waters, which covereth thee? <div eID="gen7840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7841" type="x-p"/> On account of this inhuman mode of action by which he has challenged the punishment of justice, snares are round about him (comp. Bildad’s picture of this fate of the evil-doer, <reference osisRef="Job.18.8-Job.18.10">Job 18:8-10</reference>), destruction encompasses him on every side, so that he sees no way out, and must without any escape succumb to it. And the approaching ruin makes itself known to him time after time by terrors which come suddenly upon him and disconcert him; so that his outward circumstances being deranged and his mind discomposed, he has already in anticipation to taste that which is before him. In <reference osisRef="Job.22.11">Job 22:11</reference>, לא תראה is by no means to be taken as an eventual circumstantial clause, whether it is translated affirmatively: or darkness (covers thee), that thou canst not see; or interrogatively: or does darkness (surround thee), that thou seest not? In both cases the verb in the principal clause is wanting; apart from the new turn, which או introduces, being none, it would then have to be explained with Löwenthal: or has the habit of sinning already so dulled thy feeling and darkened thine eye, that thou canst not perceive the enormity of thy transgression? But this is a meaning forced from the words which they are not capable of; it must have been at least או חשׁך בּעדך, or something similar. Since או חשׁך (to be accented without <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> with <hi type="italic">Mûnach, Dechî</hi>) cannot form a principal clause of itself, תראה is without doubt the verb belonging to it: or (או as <reference osisRef="Job.16.3">Job 16:3</reference>) seest thou not darkness? Because, according to his preceding speeches, Job does not question the magnitude of his sufferings, but acknowledges them in all their fearfulness; therefore Hahn believes it must be explained: or shouldst thou really not be willing to see thy sins, which encompass thee as thick dark clouds, which cover thee as floods of water? The two figures, however, can only be understood of the destruction which entirely shrouds Job in darkness, and threatens to drown him. But destruction, in the sense in which Eliphaz asks if Job does not see it, is certainly intended differently to what it was in Job’s complaints. Job complains of it as being unmerited, and therefore mysterious; Eliphaz, on the other hand, is desirous that he should open his eyes that he may perceive in this darkness of sorrow, this flood of suffering, the well-deserved punishment of his heinous sins, and anticipate the worst by penitence. לא תכסּךּ is a relative clause, and belongs logically also to חשׁך, comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.60.2">Isa 60:2</reference>, where שׁפעת is also found in <reference osisRef="Job.22.6">Job 22:6</reference> (from שׁפע, <hi type="italic">abundare;</hi> comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">šf‛ ,</hi> ספק, <reference osisRef="Job.20.22">Job 20:22</reference>). Eliphaz now insinuates that Job denies the special providence of God, because he doubts the exceptionless, just government of God. In the second strophe he has explained his affliction as the result of his uncharitableness; now he explains it as the result of his unbelief, which is now become manifest.
entries.1ca67005349f62ed123249a45d8ea0d0b8723451: <reference osisRef="Job.22.12-Job.14.12">Job 22:12-14 12</reference>  Is not Eloah high as the heavens? <div eID="gen7841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7842" type="x-p"/> See but the head of the stars, how exalted! 13  So then thou thinkest: “What doth God know? <div eID="gen7842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7843" type="x-p"/> Can He judge through the thick cloud? 14  Clouds veil Him that He seeth not, <div eID="gen7843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7844" type="x-p"/> And in the vault of heaven He walketh at His pleasure.” <div eID="gen7844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7845" type="x-p"/> Because Job has denied the distribution of worldly fortune, of outward prosperity and adversity, according to the law of the justice that recompenses like for like, Eliphaz charges him with that unbelief often mentioned in the Psalms (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.11">Psa 73:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.7">Psa 94:7</reference>; comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.29.15">Isa 29:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">Eze 8:12</reference>), which denies to the God in heaven, as Epicurus did to the gods who lead a blessed life in the spaces between the worlds, a knowledge of earthly things, and therefore the preliminary condition for a right comprehension of them. The mode of expression here is altogether peculiar. גּבהּ שׁמים is not <hi type="italic">acc. loci,</hi> as the like accusatives in combination with the verb שׁכן, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa 57:15</reference>, may be taken: the substantival clause would lead one to expect בּגבהּ, or better בּגבהי (<reference osisRef="Job.11.8">Job 11:8</reference>); it is rather (similar to <reference osisRef="Job.11.8">Job 11:8</reference>) <hi type="italic">nomin. praedicati:</hi> Eloah is the height of the heavens = heaven-high, as high as the heavens, therefore certainly highly, and indeed very highly, exalted above this earth. In this sense it is continued with <hi type="italic">Waw explic.:</hi> and behold (= behold then) the head of the stars, that, or how (כּי as in <reference osisRef="Gen.49.15">Gen 49:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.29">1Sa 14:29</reference>, <hi type="italic">quod</hi> = <hi type="italic">quam</hi>) exalted they are. וּראה has <hi type="italic">Asla</hi> (<hi type="italic">Kadma</hi>) in correct texts, and רמו is written רמּוּ (<hi type="italic">râmmu</hi>) with a so-called Dag. <hi type="italic">affectuosum</hi> (Olsh. §83, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). It may be received as certain that ראשׁ, the head (<hi type="italic">vertex</hi>), beside ראה (not ספר), does not signify the sum (Aben-Ezra). But it is questionable whether the genitive that follows ראשׁ is <hi type="italic">gen. partitivus:</hi> the highest among the stars (Ew., Hirz., Schlottm.), or <hi type="italic">gen. epexegeticus:</hi> the head, i.e., (in relation to the rest of the universe) the height, which is formed by the stars, or even which they occupy (Ges. <hi type="italic">coelum stellatum</hi>); the partitive rendering is to be preferred, for the Semitic perception recognises, as the plural שׁמים implies, nearer and more distant celestial spheres. The expression “head of the stars” is therefore somewhat like <hi type="italic">fastigium coeli</hi> (the extreme height, i.e., the middle of the vault of heaven), or <hi type="italic">culmen aereum</hi> (of the aether separating the strata of air above); the summit of the stars rising up into the extremest spheres is intended (we should say: the fixed stars, or to use a still more modern expression, the milky way), as also the רמו naturally refers to ראשׁ כוכבים as one notion (<hi type="italic">summitas astrorum</hi> = <hi type="italic">summa astra</hi>). <div eID="gen7845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7846" type="x-p"/> The connection of what follows with Waw is not adversative (Hirz., Ew., and others: and yet thou speakest), it is rather consecutive (Hahn: and since thou speakest; better: and in consequence of this thou speakest; or: thus speakest thou, thinkest thou then). The undeniable truth that God is exalted, and indeed absolute in His exaltation, is misapplied by Job to the false conclusion: what does God know, or (since the <hi type="italic">perf.</hi> in interrogative sentences frequently corresponds to the Latin conjunctive, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.11.3">Psa 11:3</reference>) how should God know, or take knowledge, i.e., of anything that happens on earth? In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.22.13">Job 22:13</reference></hi> the potential takes the place of this modal perfect: can He rule judicially behind the dark clouds, i.e., over the world below from which He is shut out? בּעד (of like verbal origin with the Arab. <hi type="italic">b‛da , post,</hi> prop. distance, separation, succession, but of wider use) signifies here, as in <reference osisRef="Job.1.10">Job 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.7">Job 9:7</reference>, behind, <hi type="italic">pone,</hi> with the secondary notion of being encompassed or covered by that which shuts off. Far from having an unlimited view of everything earthly from His absolute height, it is veiled from His by the clouds, so that He sees not what occurs here below, and unconcerned about it He walks the circle of the heavens (that which vaults the earth, the inhabitants of which seem to Him, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.40.22">Isa 40:22</reference>, as grasshoppers); התלּך is here, after the analogy of <hi type="italic">Kal,</hi> joined with the accus. of the way over which He walks at His pleasure: <hi type="italic">orbem coelum obambulat.</hi> By such unworthy views of the Deity, Job puts himself on a par with the godless race that was swept away by the flood in ancient days, without allowing himself to be warned by this example of punishment.
entries.ebb9b37cb0bc821a78091e8a6ae3ae7bee319632: <reference osisRef="Job.22.15-Job.18.15">Job 22:15-18 15</reference> Wilt thou observe the way of the ancient world, <div eID="gen7846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7847" type="x-p"/> Which evil men have trodden, 16 Who were withered up before their time, <div eID="gen7847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7848" type="x-p"/> Their foundation was poured out as a stream, 17 Who said unto God: Depart from us! <div eID="gen7848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7849" type="x-p"/> And what can the Almighty do to them? 18 And notwithstanding He had filled their houses with good- <div eID="gen7849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7850" type="x-p"/> The counsel of the wicked be far from me! <div eID="gen7850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7851" type="x-p"/> While in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.24">Psa 139:24</reference> דרך עולם prospectively signifies a way of eternal duration (comp. <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.20">Eze 26:20</reference>, עם עולם, of the people who sleep the interminably long sleep of the grave), ארח עולם signifies here retrospectively the way of the ancient world, but not, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jer 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.15">Jer 18:15</reference>, the way of thinking and acting of the pious forefathers which put their posterity to shame, but of a godless race of the ancient world which stands out as a terrible example to posterity. Eliphaz asks if Job will observe, i.e., keep (שׁמר as in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.22">Psa 18:22</reference>), this way trodden by people (מתי, comp. אנשׁי, <reference osisRef="Job.34.36">Job 34:36</reference>) of wickedness. Those worthless ones were withered up, i.e., forcibly seized and crushed, ולא־עת, when it was not yet time (ולא after the manner of a circumstantial clause: <hi type="italic">quum nondum,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Ps.139.16">Psa 139:16</reference>), i.e., when according to God’s creative order their time was not yet come. On קמּטוּ,<note placement="foot">This קמטו, according to the Masora, is the middle word of the book of Job (חצי הספר).</note> vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.16.8">Job 16:8</reference>; lxx correctly, συνελήφθησαν ἄωροι, nevertheless συλλαμβάνειν is too feeble as a translation of קמט; for as Arab. <hi type="italic">qbṣ</hi> signifies to take with the tip of the finer, whereas Arab. <hi type="italic">qbḍ</hi> signifies to take with the whole bent hand, so קמט, in conformity to the dull, emphatic final consonant, signifies “to bind firmly together.” In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.22.16">Job 22:16</reference></hi> יוּצק is not <hi type="italic">perf. Pual</hi> for יצּק (Ew. §83, <hi type="italic">b</hi>), for this exchange, contrary to the law of vowels, of the sharp form with the lengthened form is without example; it must at least have been written יוּצּק (comp. Jdg 18:29). It is <hi type="italic">fut. Hoph.,</hi> which, according to <reference osisRef="Job.11.15">Job 11:15</reference>, might be יצּק; here, however, it is with a resolving, not assimilation, of the <hi type="italic">Jod,</hi> as in Lev 21:10. The <hi type="italic">fut.</hi> has the signification of the imperfect which it acquires in an historic connection. It is not to be translated: their place became a stream which has flowed away (Hirz.), for the היה which would be required by such an interpretation could not be omitted; also not: <hi type="italic">flumen effusum est in fundamentum eorum</hi> (Rosenm., Hahn, and others), which would be ליסודם, and would still be very liable to be misunderstood; also not: whose foundation was a poured-out stream (Umbr., Olsh.), for then there would be one attributive clause inserted in the other; but: their solid ground became fluid like a stream (Ew., Hlgst., Schlottm.), so that נהר, after the analogy of the verbs with two accusative, Ges. §139, 2, is a so-called second acc. of the obj. which by the passive becomes a nominative (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.28.2">Job 28:2</reference>), although it might also be an apposition of the following subj. placed first: a stream (as such, like such a one) their solid ground was brought into a river; the ground on which they and their habitations stood was placed under water and floated away: without doubt the flood is intended; reference to this perfectly accords with the patriarchal pre-and extra-Israelitish standpoint of the book of Job; and the generation of the time of the flood (דור המבול) is accounted in the holy scriptures of the Old and New Testament as a paragon of godlessness, the contemporaries of Noah are the απειθοῦντες, סוררים, κατ ̓ ἐξοχήν (comp. 1Pe 3:20 with <reference osisRef="Ps.68.19">Psa 68:19</reference>). <div eID="gen7851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7852" type="x-p"/> Accordingly they are now here also further described (<reference osisRef="Job.22.17">Job 22:17</reference>) as those who said to God, “Depart from us,” and what could the Almighty do to them (למו instead of לנוּ, which was to be expected, since, as in <reference osisRef="Job.19.28">Job 19:28</reference>, there is a change from the <hi type="italic">oratio directa</hi> to <hi type="italic">obliqua</hi>)! Olshausen explains with Hahn: “with respect to what thou sayest: and what then does the Almighty do to them (for it)? He fills their houses with prosperity, while the counsel of the wicked is far from me (notwithstanding I am unfortunate).” But this explanation is as forced (since ומה without a אמרת or תאמר standing with it is taken as the word of Job) as it is contrary to the syntax (since the circumstantial clause with והוא is not recognised, and on the other hand ועצת וגו, instead of which it ought at least to have been וּממּנּי וגו, is regarded as such an one). No indeed, just this is an exceedingly powerful effect, that Eliphaz describes those godless ones who dismiss God with סור ממנו, to whom, according to Job’s assertion, Job 21:13., undimmed prosperity is portioned out, by referring to a memorable fact as that which has fallen under the strict judgment of God; and that with the very same words with which Job, <reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference>, declines communion with such prosperous evil-doers: “the counsel of the wicked be far from me,” he will have nothing more to do, not with the wicked alone, but, with a side glance at Job, even with those who place themselves on a level with them by a denial of the just government of God in the world. פּעל ל, as the following circumstantial clause shows, is intended like <reference osisRef="Ps.68.29">Psa 68:29</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.31.20">Job 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.12">Isa 26:12</reference> : how can the Almighty then help or profit them? Thus they asked, while He had filled their houses with wealth - Eliphaz will have nothing to do with this contemptible misconstruction of the God who proves himself so kind to those who dwell below on the earth, but who, though He is rewarded with ingratitude, is so just. The truly godly are not terrified like <reference osisRef="Job.17.8">Job 17:8</reference>, that retributive justice is not to be found in God’s government of the world; on the contrary, they rejoice over its actual manifestation in their own case, which makes them free, and therefore so joyous.
entries.7a6cd00eb2cbe6052bad451e94ca049050b9348e: <reference osisRef="Job.22.19-Job.20.19">Job 22:19-20 19</reference>  The righteous see it and rejoice, <div eID="gen7852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7853" type="x-p"/> And the innocent mock at them: 20  “Verily our opponent is destroyed, <div eID="gen7853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7854" type="x-p"/> And the fire hath devoured their abundance.” <div eID="gen7854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7855" type="x-p"/> This thought corresponds to that expressed as a wish, hope, or anticipation at the close of many of the Psalms, that the retributive justice of God, though we may have to wait a long time for it, becomes at length the more gloriously manifest to the joy of those hitherto innocently persecuted, Psa 58:11. The obj. of יראוּ, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.107.42">Psa 107:42</reference>, is this its manifestation. למו is not an ethical dative, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.80.7">Psa 80:7</reference>, but as in <reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">Psa 2:4</reference> refers to the ungodly whose mocking pride comes to such an ignominious end. What follow in <reference osisRef="Job.22.20">Job 22:20</reference> are the words of the godly; the introductory לאמר is wanting, as e.g., Psa 2:3. אם־לא can signify neither <hi type="italic">si non,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Job.9.24">Job 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.25">Job 24:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.31">Job 31:31</reference>, nor <hi type="italic">annon,</hi> as in a disjunctive question, <reference osisRef="Job.17.2">Job 17:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.25">Job 30:25</reference>; it is affirmative, as <reference osisRef="Job.1.11">Job 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.2.5">Job 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.36">Job 31:36</reference> - an Amen to God’s peremptory judgment. On נכחד (he is drawn away, put aside, become annulled), vid., <hi type="italic">supra,</hi> p. 398. קימנוּ (for which Aben-Ezra is also acquainted with the reading קימנוּ with קמץ קטן, i.e., צירי) has a pausal <hi type="italic">â</hi> springing from <hi type="italic">ê</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Job.20.27">Job 20:27</reference>, מתקוממה for מתקוממה; Rth 3:2, לרמותנו; <reference osisRef="Isa.47.10">Isa 47:10</reference>, ראני (together with the reading ראני, comp. <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.17">1Ch 12:17</reference>, לרמותני). The form קים is remarkable; it may be more readily taken as <hi type="italic">part. pass.</hi> (like שׂים, <hi type="italic">positus</hi>) than as <hi type="italic">nom. infin.</hi> (the act of raising for those who raise themselves); perhaps the original text had קמינו (קמינוּ). יתרם is no more to be translated their remnant (Hirz.) here than in <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Psa 17:14</reference>, at least not in the sense of <reference osisRef="Exod.23.11">Exo 23:11</reference>; that which exceeds the necessity is intended, their surplus, their riches. It is said of Job in <hi type="italic">b. Megilla,</hi> 28 <hi type="italic">a</hi>: איוב ותרן בממוניה הוה, he was extravagant (<hi type="italic">prodigus</hi>) with his property. The fire devouring the wealth of the godless is an allusion to the misfortune which has befallen him. <div eID="gen7855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7856" type="x-p"/> After this terrible picture, Eliphaz turns to the exhortation of him who may be now perhaps become ripe for repentance.
entries.fdf6dcc47f0e6804351230728de8fd150df65cb0: Job 22:21-25 21  Make friends now with Him, so hast thou peace; <div eID="gen7856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7857" type="x-p"/> Thereby good will come unto thee. 22  Receive now teaching from His mouth, <div eID="gen7857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7858" type="x-p"/> And place His utterances in thy heart. 23  If thou returnest to the Almighty, thou shalt be built up again; <div eID="gen7858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7859" type="x-p"/> If thou puttest away iniquity far from thy tents. 24  And lay by in the dust the gold ore, <div eID="gen7859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7860" type="x-p"/> And under the pebbles of the brooks the gold of Ophir. 25  So shall the Almighty be to thee gold ore in abundance, <div eID="gen7860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7861" type="x-p"/> And silver to thee of the brightest lustre. <div eID="gen7861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7862" type="x-p"/> The relationship of the verbs סכן, שׁכן, and Arab. <hi type="italic">sakana ,</hi> has been already discussed on <reference osisRef="Job.22.2">Job 22:2</reference> : the <hi type="italic">Hiph.</hi> signifies to be on friendly terms with any one; to enter into, or to stand in, an intimate relationship to any one (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.3">Psa 139:3</reference>); then also (as the Greek φιλεῖν) to get accustomed to, to be used to (Num 22:30). The second <hi type="italic">imper.</hi> is consecutive, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Prov.3.4">Pro 3:4</reference> : and have as the result of it peace (Arab. <hi type="italic">fa'âslam</hi>) = so shalt thou have peace, Ges. §130, 2. In <reference osisRef="Job.22.21">Job 22:21</reference> the first thing to be done is to clear up the form תּבואתך or (according to another reading which is likewise well attested) תּבואתך. Olshausen (in Hirz. and in his <hi type="italic">Gramm.</hi>) and Rödiger (in <hi type="italic">Thes.</hi> p. 11, <hi type="italic">suppl.</hi>) explain this form the same as the other forms which come under consideration in connection with it, viz., תּבואתה (<hi type="italic">veniat</hi>), <reference osisRef="Deut.33.16">Deu 33:16</reference>, and ותּבאתי, <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> ותּבאת (<hi type="italic">et venisses,</hi> addressed to Abigail), <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.34">1Sa 25:34</reference>, as errors in writing; whereas Ew., §191, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, sees in תּבואתך the erroneous form תּבואה = תּבוא with a superfluous feminine termination, in תּבואתה an extension of the double feminine by the unaccented <hi type="italic">ah</hi> of intention, and in תּבאתי a transfer of the inflexion of the perf. to the fut. Confining ourselves to the form which occurs here, we refer to what was said above: תבואתך is not a <hi type="italic">forma mixta </hi>from תּבואך and בּאתך, but the mistaken double feminine תּבואה with suff., the <hi type="italic">ah</hi> of which, although the tone is on the <hi type="italic">penult.,</hi> is not <hi type="italic">He voluntativum,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Isa 5:19</reference>, but <hi type="italic">He femin.</hi> The exception of such double feminines is made as certain in Hebrew by the regular form נגלתה ( = נגלת with a second feminine termination), and by examples like <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Pro 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.20">Eze 23:20</reference>, and also <reference osisRef="Josh.6.17">Jos 6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.26">2Sa 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.3">Amo 4:3</reference> (comp. even Olsh. in his <hi type="italic">Gramm.</hi> S. 449), as the double plural and its further formation by a feminine termination in Arabic. It is therefore unnecessary, with Olsh. and Röd., after the precedent of the ancient versions, to read תּבוּאתך (which is found in 19 Codd. in de Rossi): <hi type="italic">proventus tuus bonus erit.</hi> The suff. in בּהם, as <reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Isa 64:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.18">Eze 23:18</reference>, comp. עליהם, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.16">Isa 38:16</reference>, is intended as neuter, as the fem. is used elsewhere (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.38.16">Isa 38:16</reference>, בּהן): by it, i.e., by such conduct, good (prosperity) shall come to thee, and indeed, as the בוא construed with the acc. implies, in a sudden change of thy previous lot, coming about without any further effort on thy part. In the certainty that it is God’s word which he presents to his friend (the very certainty which Eliphaz also expresses elsewhere, e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.15.11">Job 15:11</reference>), he further admonishes him (<reference osisRef="Job.22.22">Job 22:22</reference>) to receive instruction from God’s mouth (מפּיו as <reference osisRef="Prov.2.6">Pro 2:6</reference>), and to allow His (God’s) utterances a place in his heart, not to let them die away without effect, but to imprint them deeply on his mind.
entries.16293e24a49854a91c1f0d878e8183243ff9c34b: Job 22:26-30 26  For then thou shalt delight thyself in the Almighty, <div eID="gen7864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7865" type="x-p"/> And lift up they countenance to Eloah; 27  If thou prayest to Him, He will hear thee, <div eID="gen7865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7866" type="x-p"/> And thou shalt pay thy vows. 28  And thou devisest a plan, and it shall be established to thee, <div eID="gen7866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7867" type="x-p"/> And light shineth upon thy ways. 29  If they are cast down, thou sayest, “Arise!” <div eID="gen7867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7868" type="x-p"/> And him that hath low eyes He saveth. 30  He shall rescue him who is not guiltless, <div eID="gen7868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7869" type="x-p"/> And he is rescued by the purity of thy hands. כּי־אז might also be translated “then indeed” (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.11.15">Job 11:15</reference>), as an emphatic resumption of the promissory והיה (<hi type="italic">tum erit</hi>), <reference osisRef="Job.22.25">Job 22:25</reference>; but what follows is really the confirmation of the promise that God will be to him a rich recompense for the earthly treasures that he resigns; therefore: for then thou shalt delight thyself in the Almighty (vid., the primary passage, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.4">Psa 37:4</reference>, and the dependent one, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.14">Isa 58:14</reference>; comp. <hi type="italic">infra,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.27.10">Job 27:10</reference>), i.e., He will become a source of highest, heartfelt joy to thee (על as interchanging with בּ by שׂמח). Then shall he be able to raise his countenance, which was previously depressed (נפלוּ, Gen 4:6.), in the consciousness of his estrangement from God by dearly cherished sin and unexpiated guilt, free and open, confident and joyous, to God. If he prays to Him (תּעתּיר may be thus regarded as the antecedent of a conditional clause, like יברח, <reference osisRef="Job.20.24">Job 20:24</reference>), He will hear him; and what he has vowed in prayer he will now, after that which he supplicated is granted, thankfully perform; the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. העתּיר (according to its etymon: to offer the incense of prayer) occurs only in <reference osisRef="Exod.8.10">Ex 8-10</reference> beside this passage, whereas גּזר (to cut in pieces, cut off) occurs here for the first time in the signification, to decide, resolve, which is the usual meaning of the word in the later period of the language. On ותגזר (with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi>, according to another reading with <hi type="italic">Kametz-chatuph</hi>), vid., Ges. §47, rem. 2. Moreover, the paratactic clauses of <reference osisRef="Job.22.28">Job 22:28</reference> are to be arranged as we have translated them; קוּם signifies to come to pass, as freq. (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.7.7">Isa 7:7</reference>, in connection with היה, to come into being). That which he designs (אמר) is successful, and is realized, and light shines upon his ways, so that he cannot stumble and does not miss his aim, - light like moonlight or morning light; for, as the author of the introductory Proverbs, to which we have already so often referred as being borrowed from the book of Job (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.21.24">Job 21:24</reference> with <reference osisRef="Prov.3.8">Pro 3:8</reference>), ingeniously says, ch. <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job 4:18</reference> : “The path of the righteous is as the morning light (כּאור נגהּ, comp. <reference osisRef="Dan.6.20">Dan 6:20</reference>), which shineth brighter and brighter into the height of day (i.e., noonday brightness).”

                  <ns0:p n="1">1. THen Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 35. 7. Psal. 16. 2. Luk. 17. 10.</ns0:note> Can a man be profitable unto God <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Add any thing to his Perfection or Felicity, to wit, by his Righteousness, as the next Verse shews. Why then dost thou insist so much upon thy own Righteousness, as if thou didst oblige God by it, or as if he could not without injury afflict thee who sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posest thy self to be a righteous person, though indeed thou art not so, as he saith, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5, 6, &c. but if thou wert really so, God is not thy debter for it. Or, <ns0:hi>because;</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>but;</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>yea rather:</ns0:hi> so this latter Clause is to be read without an Interrogation, and the for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer with it. A wise or good man (for these in Scripture-use are one and the same) doth much good to himself, he promotes his own Peace, and Honour, and Happiness by his Goodness; and having so great a reward for his Virtue, God is not indebted to him, but he is indebted to God for it.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> if he may be profitable, doth his good success depend thereon?</ns0:note> as <ns0:hi>b</ns0:hi> he that is wise may be profitable to himself <ns0:hi>c?</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. <ns0:hi>Is it</ns0:hi> any pleasure <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Such a pleasure as he needs for his own ease and content<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, without which he could not be happy, as appears by the foregoing and following words: For otherwise God is oft said to de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />light in the good actions of his People, to wit, so far as to approve and accept them.</ns0:note> to the Almighty, that thou art righteous?                   <ns0:p n="4">4. Will he reprove thee <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">

                     </ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. <ns0:hi>Is</ns0:hi> not thy wickedness great, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">

                  <ns0:p n="18">18. Yet he filled their houses with good <ns0:hi>things</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Yet it is true, that for a time God did prosper them, as he did thee; which also was the aggravation of their sin, and that which hastned their ruine: but at last, and in due time, God cut them off in a tremendous and exemplary manner<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> as he will also do thee, if thou dost not repent.</ns0:note>: but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 21. 16.</ns0:note> the counsel of the wicked is far from me <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">He repeats <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s words, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 21. 16. not without reflection and some kind of derision: Thou didst say so, but without sufficient reason and against thy own principle, that God carries himself indifferently towards good and bad; but I who have observed God's terrible judgments upon wicked men, have much more reason to abhor their counsels which had so sad an issue.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> the remnant <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">All that was left undestroyed in the general calamity. Or, <ns0:hi>their excellency,</ns0:hi> all their desirable and delectable things.</ns0:note> of them <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">

Renew thy acquaintance and converse with God by prayer, which thou hast restrained, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 15. 4. and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pentance for all thy sins, and true humiliation under his hand, and hearty compliance with all his Commands, and diligent care to serve and enjoy him; and be no longer estranged from God, as thou now art.</ns0:note>, and be at peace <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This is either 1. a promise, the Imperative be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing put for the Future of the Indicative Mood, <ns0:hi>and so thou shalt have peace; i. e.</ns0:hi> Prosperity and happiness: Or, rather 2. a Coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sel or Command, If God be an enemy to thee, as thou sayst he is, reconcile thy self to him by true repentance, and earnestly seek his favour and friendship, and do not provoke him further by thy false and wicked speeches of him, or by thy froward carriage to him: And whereas thou art full of unquietness and rage against God, learn to possess thy soul in patience, give over murmuring against him, and get a composed<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and quiet, and submissive mind and heart; which is called <ns0:hi>peace, Iudg.</ns0:hi> 6. 23. & 19, 20. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 57. 21.                   <ns0:p n="22">22. Receive, I pray thee, the law from his mouth <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Take the Law and Rule whereby thou governest thy thoughts and words, and whole life, not from profane Heathens, whose Opinion concerning God's Providence thou hast embraced, nor from thy own vain imaginations or violent passions, which have led thee into thy present errours and miscarriages, but from God, and from his Word, and from his Law which is written in thy own mind, and from the Doctrines and Instructions of the holy men of God; who are all of our mind in this matter.</ns0:note>, and lay up his words in thine heart <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Do not only hear them with thine ears, but let them sink into thy heart, being received there by hearty affection, and fixed by se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious and frequent, and practical consideration of them, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 119. 11. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 13. 19, <ns0:hi>&c. Luke</ns0:hi> 2. 19, 51.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 8. 5, 6. & 11. 13.</ns0:note> If thou return to the Almighty <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>home to the Almighty;</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>so as to reach to the Almighty</ns0:hi> and be joyned to him. The Hebrew Phrase is extraordinary, and em<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phatical, and implies a thorough and effectual turning not only from sin (which an Hypocrite may do in great part at least for a time upon carnal Motives, and without any respect or love to God) but also unto God, so as to love him and cleave to him, and sincerely devote a man's self to his fear and service. And he expresseth it in this manner, because he thought <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> to be an Hy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pocrite, and therefore counselleth him to turn to God in another and better manner than he had done; to wit, with all his heart, and not feignedly.</ns0:note>, thou shalt be built up <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">God who hath pulled thee down in thy Estate and Honour, and Children, will repair thy Ruines, and give thee more Children, which is oft called <ns0:hi>building;</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 16. 2. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 1. 21. <ns0:hi>Ruth.</ns0:hi> 4. 11. and bless thee with prosperity and happi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, as <ns0:hi>building</ns0:hi> signifies, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 42. 10. & 31. 4.</ns0:note>, thou shalt put away iniquity far from thy tabernacles <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">This may be ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther 1. a Condition upon which God makes the following Promi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses, If (which Particle may be repeated out of the former part of the Verse) <ns0:hi>thou shalt put away,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> If thou shalt effectually purge thy self and family from all sin, and keep thy self and them, as far as thou canst, from all appearances and occasions of sin<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> which is the duty of all, and the practice of true Penitents. Whereby he seems to reflect upon <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> as if he had been faulty and negligent in the government of himself or Children, notwithstand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing his sacrificing for them, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 1. Or rather 2. a Promise, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause the Conditions required had been expressed together, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21, 22. and in the beginning of this Verse, after which he comes to the Promises, and begins with this, <ns0:hi>thou shalt be built up,</ns0:hi> and so proceeds to other Promises; and therefore it seems not probable that he should return to the Conditions again, and mix the Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ditions and Promises together, which he hath so carefully sepa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rated in these Verses. And so it is either 1. a spiritual Promise, If thou dost sincerely repent, God will give thee more grace effectually to reform thy self and family, according to that rule, <ns0:hi>To him that hath, shall be given.</ns0:hi> Or 2. a temporal Promise, <ns0:hi>Thou shalt put away iniquity</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>injury,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>perverseness (i. e.</ns0:hi> either perverse and injurious men: Or God's judgments, or the punishments of thy sins; as iniquity is very oft used) <ns0:hi>far from thy tabernacles; i. e.</ns0:hi> from all thy Dwellings, and Tents, and Possessions; no hand of violence shall come near them, no evil plague shall come upon thy own habitation, or upon the habitations of thy Children, as lately it did for thine and their sins.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:note> as the stones <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">As plentifully as if the pieces of Gold were but so many pebble stones, which are to be found in and near every Brook.                   <ns0:p n="26">26.                         <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Look up to him by meditation and prayer, not as now thou dost, with horrour and grief, which is signified by a dejected Countenance, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 22. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 18. 13. but with chearfulness and confidence, as this Phrase oft notes, as <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 21. 28.                   <ns0:p n="27">27. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 50. 14, 15.</ns0:note> Thou shalt make thy prayer unto him, and he shall hear thee <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">

                  <ns0:p n="29">29. When <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> are cast down <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>When they (i. e.</ns0:hi> they who do this work.                         <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> God, <ns0:hi>unto whom onely salvation belongeth, Psalm</ns0:hi> 3. 8.</ns0:note> shall save <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Either 1. e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ternally; or 2. temporally; to wit, from the evils here mentioned.</ns0:note>
